statescope

Per-layer dictionaries for the language model Qwen3.5-0.8B: a state dictionary of the residual stream and an MLP dictionary of gated low-rank transforms at each of its 24 layers, a reader in one Python file, and one computation followed through named units.

Base model
Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B24 layers, width 1024
Published
2026-11-20set frozen on 2026-11-18
Code
mconcat/statescopeon GitHub, MIT
Weights
mconcat/statescope-qwen3.5-0.8bon Hugging Face, MIT, about 27.4 GiB

statescope is a reader in one Python file and a set of dictionary weights for Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B. Each of the model's 24 layers has two dictionaries that were trained separately. The state dictionary writes the residual stream as a few active groups of directions. The MLP dictionary writes the layer's MLP as a sum of small gated linear operations called transforms.

This page follows one computation through these units: how the model decides to break a line in text wrapped to a fixed width. One transform at layer 8 fires on the first token of each line. A head of the layer-9 mixer carries the count of characters since then. Two transforms at layer 9 turn the count into the line-break decision: one is on while the line is short, and the other is on once it is long. In text wrapped at 60 characters, swapping only the first transform's write through the mixer carries 0.328 of the change in the model's preference for a line break, and swapping the whole layer-8 MLP output the same way carries 0.353.

The evidence is narrow. The set covers one model and one dictionary seed, and it has no dictionaries for the mixers. The demonstration covers one easy task with dedicated MLP neurons and is not evidence that dictionary units are better than neurons. The trainers are not in the repository, and the per-layer numbers cannot be recomputed from the published files. The section Limits lists all of this.

Two dictionaries per layer

The base model has 24 layers and width 1024. Each layer has a mixer, which is its GatedDeltaNet or attention sublayer, and an MLP. Each layer has a state dictionary and an MLP dictionary that were trained separately. Figure 2 shows where each one reads.

The state dictionary represents the residual stream at two sites of its layer. A residual stream site is a location between the mixer and the MLP or after the MLP where a state dictionary reads the residual stream. The site resid_mid.L is the input of the norm before the MLP. The site resid_post.L is resid_mid plus the MLP output.

The MLP dictionary represents the layer's MLP operations, taking the post-norm MLP input and reconstructing the raw MLP output. It uses the sparse mixture of linear transforms, or MOLT, from the public crosslayer-transcoder code.

In the state dictionary, the input is divided by its own size, and it is then standardised with a mean vector and one scale per site. Each layer's dictionary was trained on 30,003,200 tokens over 7,325 steps.

The MLP dictionary uses a JumpReLU gate. Each transform has free read and write matrices. There is no skip connection. Training uses a tanh sparsity penalty. Training used 58,600 steps of 500 tokens, or 29.3 million tokens, per layer. The learning rate was 4.0e-05. The sparsity penalty coefficient was 7.5e-05 for layers 0 to 22. Layer 23 used 2.5e-05 in a separate run.

No mixer dictionaries. This set contains no dictionaries for the mixers. Where the example below passes through a mixer, it is measured in the model's own mixer.

The set contains 144 weight and config files. State dictionaries occupy about 12.0 GiB, and MLP dictionaries occupy about 15.4 GiB. The repository contains the reader, a demonstration and tests. The trainers for this set are not in the repository.

A worked example: when to break a line

The task uses texts wrapped to a fixed width. At the last word of a line, the model must predict a line break, so it must know how many characters the line already holds. Figure 1 shows three dictionary units that follow this count on one text.

The original project found the chain described in this section. The script demo/line_count.py uses its chosen transform, group and head and re-measures their effects. It does not search for them. The shares, firing rates and per-item margins on this page are the output of one run of that script, read from its result.json and result.safetensors. No model runs in the browser.

Pairs of texts and the margin

Each item pairs 256-token texts ending on the same words. In every cell, the clean text's last line is full, at most 6 characters short of the width, so a line break is due. In the corrupt text a line break is not due.

A cell is a task setting defined by the wrapping width and how the corrupt text is made. The three cells are count:60, count:100 and width:100. Each cell contains 64 pairs.

  • In the count cells, the corrupt text's last line starts at a later word than the clean text's, chosen so that the line holds between 35% and 65% of the width at the last word, and the preceding lines are wrapped backward from that word at the same width, moving their line breaks too.
  • In the width cell, the corrupt text's last line starts at the same word as the clean text's, and the preceding lines are wrapped backward at 1.75 times the width.

The margin is the last-token logsumexp of newline-token logits minus the logsumexp of logits for tokens starting with a space. A higher margin favours a line break.

m = logsumexp(logits of newline tokens) - logsumexp(logits of tokens that start with a space)

A patch replaces a tensor in the clean run with a value built from the corrupt run and moved onto the clean run's token positions. Each row called a swap on this page is one such patched run of the clean texts. A share is the part of the clean/corrupt margin difference carried by the patched tensor. A share of 0 means that the patch changes nothing. A share of 1 means that the patch alone turns the clean run into the corrupt one.

share = mean(m_clean - m_patched) / mean(m_clean - m_corrupt)

The chain, step by step

  1. Transform 189 of the L8 MLP dictionary fires on the first token of a line. Its write lies mostly inside the frame of state group 11586 of resid_post.8, the first-token-of-a-line group.
  2. The model's L9 mixer reads that write. Swapping only transform 189's write or only group 11586 moves the answer about as much as swapping the whole L8 MLP output in the count cells. GatedDeltaNet head 10 carries the count inside the mixer.
  3. Transforms 410 and 1749 of the L9 MLP dictionary turn the count into the line-break decision. Transform 410 is on while the line is short, and transform 1749 is on once it is long. What the L9 transforms read of the mixer's write lies mostly inside the 4-dimensional frame of state group 4885 of resid_mid.9.

An easy task. This is an easy task for which the model has dedicated MLP neurons. The demonstration is not evidence that dictionary units are better than neurons.

Figure 4 ties each step to its swaps. In every step, the swap of one named unit stands next to the swap of the whole tensor it belongs to, measured by the same route.

In the count cells, transform 189 or group 11586 carries about as much as the whole L8 MLP output through the L9 mixer. Head 10's read alone gives a larger share than the whole mixer output. Transform 410 carries the L9 MLP's effect in count:60, and transform 1749 carries it in width:100.

Transform 189 fires on 1.000 of line-first tokens, 0.001 of line-break tokens and 0.010 of other tokens. Of the energy in its swapped write, 0.769 lies inside group 11586's frame. The largest value among five random frames is 0.016. The chance value for a 4-dimensional frame in 1,024 dimensions is 0.004.

Transform 410 fires on 0.84 to 0.89 of tokens when a line holds 20 to 49 characters. It fires on 0.25 at 60 to 69 characters and 0.03 at 70 to 79. Transform 1749 fires on 0.00 below 70 characters, 0.19 at 80 to 89 and 0.60 at 90 to 99.

The original project ranked transforms on the odd-numbered items and reads results on the even-numbered ones, 32 items per cell. Some groups were first chosen after looking at all items; when the original project repeated the selection on odd-numbered items only, the chosen groups, frames and transforms were the same. Head 10 was known from earlier work.

One swap, item by item

A share is a ratio of two means over items. Figure 5 shows what is behind one share: for each of the 64 items of a cell, the margin of the clean run, of the corrupt run, and of the clean run with one swap.

Rounding. Single-item margins of dictionary swaps are reproducible only to about 0.1. Shares are reproducible only to about 0.003. A patched tensor is rounded to bf16. A 1e-6 relative difference between implementations flips some rounded elements.

From the L9 mixer to the L9 transforms

The last link asks how the mixer's write reaches the L9 transforms. The whole mixer swap and head 10's swap are each applied in full, only inside the 4-dimensional frame of state group 4885 of resid_mid.9, or as the rest. The share is then read by three routes. For the first two, the changed resid_mid.9 enters the L9 MLP dictionary, and only the change in the selected transforms' writes is patched at the MLP output: once for the six L9 transforms selected by the original project (410, 1749, 6, 3720, 1394 and 2275), and once for transforms 410 and 1749 alone. The third route is the same change with everything downstream.

The part inside group 4885's frame moves the transforms about as much as the whole swap. The rest moves them little. On even-numbered items, for the whole mixer swap, the rest carries 0.016 in count:60, 0.032 in count:100 and 0.042 in width:100 through the six transforms. Through the two transforms alone, the rest carries 0.013, 0.052 and 0.031. A random 4-dimensional frame carries at most 0.005 through the six transforms and 0.007 through the two.

Group 4885 is dense. State group 11586 is sparse, but not every group is sparse. Some groups encountered by the original project on this task are dense 4-dimensional coordinates active on most tokens. They carry information in their coordinates. Group 4885 is one of these dense groups, not a sparse feature.

With everything downstream, the rest carries 0.156 in count:60, 0.168 in count:100 and 0.177 in width:100. The frame is therefore not the only route to the answer. The downstream shares of the two parts do not add up to the whole.

The original project registered a pass rule for the mixer-to-MLP link before measuring it. The part inside the frame must keep at least 0.75 of the whole share. The rest must keep at most 0.25 of it and at most 0.05. Random frames must carry at most 0.01. The rule applies in both count cells. The original project's verdict was that the rule holds for the route through the six transforms and holds only in part for the route through 410 and 1749 alone, because it recorded a share of 0.051 for the rest in count:100 through those two transforms.

Numbers per layer

FVU means fraction of variance unexplained. It is squared reconstruction error divided by squared deviation from the per-dimension mean of each held-out split. The state FVU is in raw residual units at the two state sites. The MLP FVU is in raw MLP output units.

Two kinds of numbers appear in Figure 7, and the figure keeps them apart. This repository measured the state FVU at both sites and the MLP FVU with its reader on all tokens of the original project's four held-out splits. The splits contain 257,122 tokens per layer, of which 179 are at position 0. Position 0 means the first position of each sequence. The original project recorded the MLP FVU at training, the MLP transforms on per token and the MLP transforms alive on a held-out shard of each layer's training capture, with position 0 included. The two MLP FVU series differ because they are measured on different tokens.

Not recomputable. The held-out activations are not published, so users cannot recompute these exact numbers. The shards behind the training-time numbers were deleted afterwards, and this repository did not repeat those measurements.

Position 0 matters for the state dictionary at some layers: at layer 6, resid_mid, the state FVU is 0.2524 with position 0 and 0.2184 without it. The original project dropped position 0 during state dictionary training and included it during MLP dictionary training. The reader's capture drops it.

Spliced-in loss

Spliced-in loss is the increase in next-token cross-entropy when a dictionary reconstruction replaces the true activation in the forward pass, one layer and one dictionary at a time. The original project measured it in nats on text with clean cross-entropy 2.808. This repository did not repeat the measurement.

The original project used FineWeb-Edu rows outside the training mixture, taking the first 100 documents of at least 256 tokens and the first 256 tokens of each. Position 0 was not replaced. Loss was averaged over positions 1 to 254, or 25,400 positions. The dictionaries are the released ones. The MLP result for layer 23 comes from a separate measurement by the original project on the same kind of web text.

In the original project's comparison on the same text, the earlier set had smaller increases at all 24 state layers and MLP layers 0 to 22. For the state dictionary at layer 9, it recorded +0.243 here against +0.161 for the earlier set. At layer 23, the released MLP dictionary had the smaller increase, +0.0502 against +0.0840 for the earlier set.

A second set, for Qwen3.5-4B

A second set for Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B, with 32 layers and width 2,560, is published at mconcat/statescope-qwen3.5-4b and occupies about 168 GiB. It uses the same forms, reader and folder layout, with ALWAYS_ON.json added and 9,920 MLP transforms per layer. Each state dictionary has 16,384 groups of 4 directions, with 24 active per token, as in the 0.8B set.

It is a copy made on 2026-11-20 of what the original project trained with one seed, rather than a frozen configuration like the 0.8B set. There is no demonstration for it; demo/line_count.py is for 0.8B only. The demonstration and the 0.8B numbers do not carry over to this set.

The limits of this set are different from those of the 0.8B set, and several are larger.

Reconstruction is worse than for 0.8B
State FVU in the middle layers is 0.31 to 0.42, against 0.25 to 0.27 for 0.8B. The 24 active groups cover 3.75% of the width of this model and 9.4% of the width of 0.8B. That this smaller fraction is the cause is an inference, not a measurement.
Spliced-in loss at one layer only
The original project measured spliced-in loss at layer 16 only. On held-out text the model itself answered, it recorded +0.303 for the state dictionary at resid_post.16 and +0.0068 for the MLP dictionary. The other layers were not measured.
24 active groups are a default, not an optimum
At layer 16, the original project recorded a spliced-in loss of +0.303, +0.171 and +0.110 with 24, 40 and 60 active groups per token. The 40- and 60-group dictionaries are not in this set.
Many transforms never fire
Many MLP transforms never fired on the original project's held-out shard, up to 60% at the last layer, where 3,974 of 9,920 were alive.
A few transforms fire on almost every token
At most layers a few transforms fire on almost every token and carry a large share of the write energy; ALWAYS_ON.json lists them. On the web text sample they carry up to 0.69 of the summed write energy, at layer 11. The count depends on the text: the counts on the web text sample and on the training-mix shard differ at 17 layers. A transform of this set must not be read as one operation without checking this list.
The penalty was chosen at one layer
The sparsity penalty 3e-05 was chosen at layer 16, where its spliced-in loss was lower than with 7.5e-05. No other layer compared penalties.
No unit of this set was read or steered here
No unit of this set was read, edited or steered by the experiments behind the 0.8B results on this page. Nothing here supports a claim that the groups or transforms of this set are interpretable. The checks of this set say that the files are built and read as defined; they are not a statement about quality.
One seed, no trainers, unpublished held-out data
The set has one training seed. No demonstration script exists for this set, and the trainers are not in the repository. The held-out activations behind this repository's FVU columns are not published, and the numbers recorded at training cannot be recomputed from the published files. The reader's capture on the 4B model was not compared with the original project's capture.

What was checked

The checks below compare this repository's reader and demonstration with the original project's code and records for the 0.8B set. All comparisons ran on one RTX 5090 machine with Qwen3.5-0.8B. Rules R8 and R9 were written and committed before the runs they judge. They show that the published files are read as the original project read them. They are not a statement about the quality of the dictionaries.

State reader against the original project's separate reader
The state reader was compared with a reader the original project wrote separately from its trainer, at 24 layers, 4 splits of 4,096 tokens and 2 sites.

Every share of the demonstration
Every demonstration share agreed with the original harness's reference run and the original project's recorded numbers: 39 swaps in 3 cells on 3 sets of items. The item file matched the original items exactly.

The published files
All 144 release files matched the manifest. MLP tensors for layers 0 to 22 were bit-identical to the training exports used by the reader tests. Layer 23 passed its own comparison with the public forward pass. No file header or config held a machine path.
A fresh download, in the tested library versions
On 2026-11-20, the code was cloned from GitHub into an empty folder and the weights were downloaded into an empty folder. With torch 2.11.0+cu128 and transformers 5.20.2, demo/line_count.py wrote a result byte-identical to the tested run.
The same download, in newer library versions
With torch 2.15.0+cu132 and transformers 5.23.0, the same demonstration was not byte-identical. The documented numbers are exact for the tested versions; newer versions moved shares by up to about 0.01.
single-item margins differ by at most 0.146shares differ by at most 0.011
Tests
All 167 tests passed: the 36 that need no private data and 131 that do. A reader of the repository can run the 36 with pytest -m "not legacy".

Every comparison used one machine and one GPU model, RTX 5090. A second machine and a different GPU model were not checked.

Limits

These limits belong to the results above and should be read with them.

One model and one dictionary seed
The set covers one model, 0.8B, and one dictionary seed. The demonstration covers the same model and seed, with texts wrapped to a fixed width.
No dictionaries for the mixers
There are no dictionaries for the mixers, which are the GatedDeltaNet and attention sublayers. The count of characters is carried inside the L9 mixer, so that step of the chain is measured in the model's own mixer and head 10, not in a dictionary.
An easy task with dedicated MLP neurons
This is an easy task for which the model has dedicated MLP neurons. The demonstration is not evidence that dictionary units are better than neurons.
The script does not search
The script uses the original project's chosen transform, group and head and re-measures their effects. It does not search for them.
Group 4885 is dense
State group 11586 is sparse, but not every group is sparse. Some groups encountered by the original project on this task are dense 4-dimensional coordinates active on most tokens. They carry information in their coordinates. Group 4885 is one of these dense groups, not a sparse feature.
The frame is not the only route, and the pass rule holds only in part
The frame of group 4885 is not the only route from the L9 mixer to the answer. The registered pass rule for that link holds for the route through the six transforms and holds only in part for the route through transforms 410 and 1749 alone.
Rounding of single-item margins
Single-item margins of dictionary swaps are reproducible only to about 0.1. Shares are reproducible only to about 0.003. A patched tensor is rounded to bf16. A 1e-6 relative difference between implementations flips some rounded elements. Newer library versions moved shares by up to about 0.01. A pre-activation within float rounding of its hard threshold can be on in one computation and off in another.
The trainers are not in the repository
Training cannot be reproduced because the trainers for this set are not in the repository. Porting them is planned. No full-length training run was repeated for either design.
Numbers that cannot be recomputed from the published files
The per-layer reconstruction numbers and the spliced-in loss cannot be reproduced because the held-out activations and texts behind them are not published. The original project recorded MLP FVU, transforms on per token and transforms alive at training on a held-out shard of each layer's training capture. The shards were subsequently deleted, including the shard for layer 23's separate run. This repository did not repeat the original project's training-time MLP held-out measurements or the spliced-in loss measurements.
The earlier set had smaller spliced-in loss
In the original project's comparison on the same text, the earlier set had smaller increases at all 24 state layers and MLP layers 0 to 22.
One machine and one GPU model
Every comparison ran on one machine with one RTX 5090. A second machine and a different GPU model were not checked.

Using it

Python 3.12 or newer is required. In a checkout of the code, install the reader with the packages that capture and the demonstration need, and download the weights. Replace <folder> with the destination.

sh
pip install -e '.[model]'
hf download mconcat/statescope-qwen3.5-0.8b --local-dir <folder>

The reader is the single file src/statescope/reader.py. It can be copied next to the weights. capture returns resid_mid, mlp_out and resid_post for the requested layer with position 0 dropped.

python
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from statescope.reader import StateVocab, PublicMolt, capture

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B", dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda").eval()
input_ids = torch.tensor([tokenizer("The committee met on Thursday to review the budget.")["input_ids"]], device="cuda")

V = StateVocab("<release>/state/L9", "cuda")
M = PublicMolt("<release>/mlp/L9", "cuda")
acts = capture(model, 9, input_ids)                      # resid_mid, mlp_out, resid_post; position 0 dropped
groups, codes = V.encode(acts["resid_post"], "resid_post.9")
x_hat = V.reconstruct(acts["resid_post"], "resid_post.9")
gate, y_hat = M.forward(acts["resid_mid"])               # gate (tokens, 3968), y_hat ~ acts["mlp_out"]
write = M.transform_write(acts["resid_mid"], 410)        # what transform 410 adds to the MLP output

The first command checks all 144 files against the manifest. The second re-runs the traced line-count chain; it ran in under two minutes on one RTX 5090, including model loading.

sh
python demo/verify_release.py --release <folder>
python demo/line_count.py --release <folder> --device cuda:0 --out <folder for the result>

Without flash-linear-attention, transformers silently uses a slow GatedDeltaNet reference implementation. Drop position 0 when measuring with the state dictionary. The capture function already does this.
